extracted.intended_audience: mathematics and engineering educators, curriculum designers, and researchers in undergraduate mathematics and engineering education
extracted.subtask_description: Defines what engineering faculty mean by 'mathematical maturity' for undergraduate engineering students and identifies the skills, attitudes, knowledge, and curricular alignments they consider essential. Useful for informing course design, prerequisites, and assessment of readiness for engineering coursework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical modeling skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty believe the mathematically mature student will have strong mathematical modeling skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeling competency is central: the ability to pose, simplify, represent, and solve engineering problems mathematically. Linked to representational fluency and to tasks such as model-eliciting activities and open-ended engineering problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to extract meaning from symbols (symbol sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to extract meaning from symbols and work with notation meaningfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes ‘symbol sense’ and representational ability: interpreting equations and symbols in context rather than treating them as rote manipulable entities. Faculty lament underdeveloped facility with symbols as a barrier to applying mathematics in engineering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of computational tools as needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to use computational tools appropriately as part of mathematical problem solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should know when and how to use computational resources (software, numerical methods) to support modeling and engineering practice rather than relying solely on hand calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemic beliefs about mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Students’ beliefs about the nature and value of mathematics (e.g., whether mathematics is related to the real world and has practical value).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty report that dysfunctional epistemic beliefs (thinking mathematics is unrelated to the real world) undermine modeling skills. Instruction should address and shift these beliefs by integrating physical context and realistic examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity to engineering experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the mathematics students use is genuine to the experience of engineering (reflects real engineering practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courses and problems should mirror engineering tasks — include realistic contexts, ill-posed problems, and solutions that resemble professional practice to improve transfer and perceived relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connecting mathematics to applications / transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: Students’ ability to perceive and make connections between taught mathematics and engineering applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty ask whether students can connect math to engineering uses and whether they see 'real life' applications; instructors should design activities that encourage explicit mapping between math and engineering contexts to improve transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solving open-ended/multi-solution problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Willingness and ability to tackle problems that have multiple correct solutions or solutions that aren’t immediately apparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty value assigning problems with multiple correct solutions and discouraging formula-following; such problems develop modeling judgment and creative problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity for long, complex problem-solving (time-on-task)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to work on multi-step problems that require substantial time (how many minutes longest problems take).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty use the length and complexity of problems as indicators of maturity; students should be able to sustain effort and reasoning across longer tasks typical in engineering problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical stance toward models
rubrics_metrics.description: Students think about models critically (questioning assumptions) rather than accepting them hegemonically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developing skeptical but informed attitudes toward models helps students select, adapt, and critique models appropriate to engineering contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention and transfer of mathematical learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether students remember and transfer what they learned in mathematics to later engineering courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty worry about lack of transfer; curricula should be sequenced and taught to promote long-term retention and applicability in later courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific procedural and declarative content mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: Mastery of particular mathematical techniques and concepts necessary for succeeding in engineering courses (e.g., integration by parts, how to define variables, understanding 'what is a scalar').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty list concrete skills and concepts students 'must' have mastered to perform well in downstream courses; prerequisites should guarantee such mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques often missing from calculus prerequisites
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical mathematical practices not commonly taught in calculus but valued in engineering (dimensional analysis, extreme case analysis, 'name that object' exercises).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These problem-framing/analysis techniques are recommended additions to better prepare students for engineering modeling tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skills at manipulating notation and working with symbols abstractly
rubrics_metrics.description: Facility manipulating notation and operating with symbols in abstract contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closely related to symbol sense: ability to manipulate and reinterpret notation, choose appropriate representations, and move between symbolic and concrete forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for graphical/intuitive vs analytic/formal methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether instruction and student reasoning favor graphical/intuitive methods or analytic/formal methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty report on encouraging graphical/intuitive reasoning in some contexts versus formal analytic solutions in others; balance affects how students apply math in engineering settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimation and approximation skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Encouraging estimation over exact calculation when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimation is a valued engineering competency (order-of-magnitude reasoning, sanity checks) and should be emphasized alongside calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventiveness: creating own methods vs reliance on formula sheets
rubrics_metrics.description: Students’ tendency to create their own methods versus being beholden to memorized formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty value students who can invent or adapt methods in novel situations rather than merely applying rote procedures from a formula sheet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on derivations
rubrics_metrics.description: The role and importance placed on derivations in the course (for practicing engineers vs researchers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty differ on whether derivations are essential for future practitioners; rubric includes considering the pedagogical value of derivations for deeper understanding versus practical competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curricular alignment between engineering and mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: The relationship and coordination between engineering curriculum and mathematics curriculum (content choice and sequencing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty discuss whether current curricula meet engineering needs and whether content order supports transfer; better alignment can reduce gaps and improve preparedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-appropriate teaching (engineers vs mathematics faculty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief that some mathematics topics or skills might be taught better by engineering faculty and others by mathematics faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty reflect on which topics (e.g., Laplace transforms) are better situated in engineering courses versus math courses and how that affects relevance and mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representational fluency (multiple representations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to use and move between multiple representations (graphs, equations, physical descriptions, simulations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representational fluency supports modeling and conceptual understanding; faculty reference the importance of students employing varied representations in problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techno-mathematical literacies
rubrics_metrics.description: Essential technological and mathematical literacies for future engineers (computational/material literacies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes familiarity with computational materials science, software tools, and literacies identified as necessary for contemporary engineering practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical disposition and attitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: Disposition toward mathematics (e.g., motivation, persistence, skeptical reverence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attitudes such as persistence, willingness to engage with hard problems, and a respectful skepticism toward mathematics are cited as parts of maturity that affect learning and application.
